title: Unburying the segregationist history of Maryland’s youth justice system
summary: A century ago, Black youth who died in state care were buried in unmarked graves. Today in Maryland, they are thrown into adult prisons. The state must do better by those youth, living and dead, write Vincent Schiraldi and Marc Schindler.
content:
by Vincent Schiraldi and Marc Schindler, Maryland Matters November 11, 2025

by Vincent Schiraldi and Marc Schindler, Maryland Matters November 11, 2025

Recent news of a long-abandoned burial site near Maryland’s House of Reformation for Colored Children – a Blacks-only youth prison opened in 1873 to remove youth from adult prisons – has sparked much-needed grappling with the state’s legacy of disparate treatment of youth of color and laws that disproportionately prosecute Black children as adults. This comes against the backdrop of actions by President Donald Trump to erase uncomfortable history, as well as to prosecute 14-year-olds as adults in Washington, D.C.

Between the 1880s and 1939 there were likely more than 230 children buried, in mostly unmarked graves, in a wooded area adjacent to the House of Reformation in Cheltenham. Before its opening, Black youth, some as young as 5, were sent to Maryland’s adult prisons. The House of Reformation opened nearly two decades after the House of Refuge – the reform school established in Baltimore to remove white children from Maryland’s adult prisons.

While records mostly cite disease as the youths’ cause of death, reporting at the time reveals violence, gross neglect and cover-ups. It appears families of the boys who died were rarely, if ever, notified. State officials were aware of the site as far back as the 1970s, but nothing was done to preserve it, even when the adjacent area was turned into an appropriately dignified cemetery for Maryland veterans.

So more than 200 Black youth, buried in unmarked graves with officials aware of the situation going back 50 years, but doing nothing. This scandal presents, as Legislative Black Caucus Chair Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) urged on a recent site visit with caucus members, “an opportunity to take action.”

Fortunately, through work done under the Moore administration and recent actions of elected officials, it appears there will finally be steps taken to address these issues.

Since locating the burial site in October 2024, the Department of Juvenile Services began plans to restore, recognize and maintain it, including: applying for funds for a ground-penetrating radar survey to discern how many boys are buried there; restoring the area as an official cemetery identifying the buried boys; attempting to communicate with the boys’ families; partnering with nonprofit groups and descendants to recognize the cemetery’s history; and creating a dignified process to address the harms against them. This was part of a larger initiative we launched to document the segregationist history of juvenile justice in Maryland under the belief that, to change the system, we had to grapple with the past, even if that was uncomfortable.

When the burial site was revealed in July, Senate Judicial Proceedings Chair Will Smith (D-Montgomery) called to rehabilitate the grounds with dignity. In stark contrast to proposals to try 14-year-olds as adults in neighboring D.C., Smith also announced he would reintroduce legislation to curb Maryland’s practice of automatically trying so many youth as adults, a reform recently endorsed by the state’s juvenile justice commission. As Smith said then, “Segregation was terrible. Secretly burying young people in unmarked graves is indefensible. But at least the leaders of that day were taking young people out of adult jails and prisons.”

Arguments in favor of Smith’s approach – and against Trump’s – are strong.  Maryland currently incarcerates a higher percentage of its youth in adult jails and prisons than any state except Alabama. The department calculated it cost nearly $20 million annually just to hold youths while they are processed in slow-moving adult courts to decide whether they stay in adult court or are returned to juvenile court. About 85% of cases were either returned to juvenile court or dismissed, begging the question of how this approach makes sense.

Additionally, research shows that prosecuting youth in the adult system not only fails to  contribute to public safety, it results in more crime. Youth prosecuted as adults are more likely to reoffend and to do so in a violent manner than similar youth kept in juvenile court. Youth held in the adult system are also more likely to be sexually assaulted and to attempt suicide.

And like the double-standard that existed when Maryland operated segregated facilities, the state’s “autowaiver” law is not affecting all children equally.  Nine out of 10 youth charged as adults are youth of color; 80% are Black.

A century ago, poor Black youth were thrown away and buried in unmarked graves. We need to acknowledge this painful history, learn from it and atone for those harms. Today the system throws them away into adult prisons despite evidence that that is ineffective and unfair.  We must do better to honor these youths’ legacies and change our laws to reflect what data shows will improve public safety, save money, and create a more equitable system.
